beef-potatoes-and-vegetables-excluding-c.title: Beef with Potatoes and Vegetables in Tomato Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of lean beef, boiled or roasted potatoes, and a variety of vegetables (such as bell pepper, zucchini, onion, and tomatoes) cooked in a flavorful tomato‑based sauce. The combination of protein, complex carbs, and vitamins makes it a nutritious and balanced meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is an excellent source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.
Tomatoes used in the sauce are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that supports heart health.
Potatoes retain most of their B‑vitamin content when steamed or baked with the skin on.
Tomatoes and bell peppers together enhance vitamin C absorption, boosting immunity.
Traditionally the dish is slow‑cooked, resulting in exceptionally tender meat.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: The meat supplies easily absorbed heme iron and zinc, supporting immune function and metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Potatoes and beef deliver B6, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy production.

items.title: Lycopene and vitamin C
items.content: The tomato sauce is rich in lycopene and vitamin C, both powerful antioxidants.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and skin‑on potatoes add fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Choosing lean cuts of beef reduces the risk of elevated cholesterol.

items.title: Sodium in the sauce
items.content: Prepared tomato sauces can be salty; monitor added salt to keep sodium intake moderate.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Potential meat pathogens
items.content: Beef should be cooked thoroughly to eliminate salmonella and other food‑borne bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, mixing beef pieces with potatoes and vegetables, and drizzling with tomato sauce. Garnish with fresh herbs (parsley or cilantro) and accompany with whole‑grain bread if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers within two hours of cooking and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. When frozen, the dish retains quality for up to 2 months.

burrito-meat-with-beans-no-cheese.title: Meat and Bean Burrito, No Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A meat and bean burrito without cheese is a Mexican dish consisting of a large soft wheat tortilla wrapped around a filling of sautéed meat, boiled beans, rice, vegetables and spices. The absence of cheese makes it less fatty and suitable for those avoiding dairy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos originated in northern Mexico where wheat flour is more common than corn.
Traditional fillings use beef, but pork, chicken or turkey are also popular.
Beans add protein and fiber, increasing the dish’s satiety.
Leaving out cheese lets the spices and fresh vegetables shine more.
Burritos are often served with salsa, guacamole or sour cream, which can be swapped for vegan sauces.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Beans supply soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat and beans are good sources of iron, important for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Low in lactose
items.content: Without cheese, the burrito is suitable for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and beans provide B6 and B12 vitamins, which aid the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces can raise the salt level; monitor added salt.

items.title: Meat fat content
items.content: Fatty cuts increase calories; choose lean cuts or trim excess fat.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: The wheat tortilla may trigger reactions in people with gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor harmful bacteria; cook thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Burritos are hand‑friendly; cut them in half and enjoy. Warm them in a microwave or skillet, add fresh veggies, salsa, guacamole or a squeeze of lime for extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared burrito in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For freezing, wrap tightly in plastic film and keep for up to 2 months; reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

cookie-oatmeal-sandwich-with-creme-filli.title: Cookie, oatmeal sandwich with creme filling

content.title: About
content.content: The cookie, oatmeal sandwich with creme filling is a two‑layer dry snack where a smooth creamy filling is sandwiched between two crunchy oatmeal cookies. It combines the nutty aroma of whole oat, a light sweetness from the cookie, and a velvety cream texture, making it a popular bite for both children and adults.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat in the cookie gives it a denser structure and boosts dietary fiber content.
The creamy filling is often made from dairy and plant oils, giving it a softer mouthfeel than traditional buttercream.
These sandwiches are frequently used in school lunchboxes because of their convenient shape and long shelf life.
In some countries they are served as mini‑portions at children’s parties.
Oats are considered heart‑healthy due to their beta‑glucan content.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Oat‑based cookies contain soluble and insoluble fibers that support normal bowel function.

items.title: Contains beta‑glucan
items.content: Beta‑glucan from oats helps lower cholesterol levels and supports immune function.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The cookie provides thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D in the creme
items.content: The creamy filling is often fortified with calcium and vitamin D, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Low in trans‑fats
items.content: Modern recipes use plant oils without trans‑fats, making the product safer for the heart.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The cookie contains wheat, so people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid it.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The sweet creme raises the overall sugar level, so those with diabetes should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The filling is often dairy‑based; lactose‑intolerant individuals should choose a lactose‑free version.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich is relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is recommended, especially on weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The cookie is convenient to eat as a standalone snack, cut into bite‑size pieces for a kids’ lunch, or paired with a cup of tea. The creme can be gently spread with a knife to make it more flowy and used as a topping for desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage (over 3 months) keep them in the refrigerator to preserve the freshness of the creme. Discard any product that develops off‑odors, discoloration, or visible mold.

content.title: About
content.content: The cookie toffee bar is a crunchy biscuit topped with a soft caramel toffee. It combines the sweet, buttery flavor of the toffee with a light, slightly buttery biscuit texture. The product is individually wrapped, making it a convenient snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The toffee bar was first launched in 1998 as a seasonal product.
The caramel layer is made from butter, sugar and cream, giving it a characteristic golden hue.
The biscuit is made from wheat flour, sugar, eggs and a small amount of leavening agent.
Each portion weighs 45 g and contains about 210 kcal.
The bar is often used as an ingredient in dessert assortments and gift baskets.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Simple carbohydrates in the toffee and biscuit provide a quick energy boost.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: The cream‑based caramel layer contributes a modest amount of calcium, beneficial for bones.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour and eggs supply vitamins B1, B2 and B6, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Gluten and dairy allergy
items.content: The biscuit contains wheat and the toffee contains dairy; people with these allergies should avoid the product.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: A large amount of sugar can contribute to tooth decay and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Regular consumption may lead to weight gain; moderation is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The cookie toffee bar can be enjoyed on its own, added to ice cream, yogurt, or used as a garnish for desserts. If desired, it can be gently warmed to soften the caramel.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place, in the original packaging or an airtight container. At temperatures above 25 °C the bar may become soft. See the package for the best‑before date.

egg-roll-with-beef-and-or-pork.title: Egg Roll with Beef and/or Pork

content.title: About
content.content: Egg roll with beef and/or pork is a classic Asian snack made from a thin wheat wrapper, a layer of egg omelette, and a filling of finely chopped beef, pork or a mix of both, seasoned with soy sauce, ginger and spices. The roll is deep‑fried until golden and served hot.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The egg roll originated in China in the early 20th century as street food.
A thin batter creates a light wrapper, while the egg adds a delicate flavor and extra protein.
In some regions the roll is served with chili sauce or sweet vinegar.
Traditional fillings often include shredded carrots, cabbage and onions.
Egg rolls are a common component of bento boxes in Japan.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef and pork provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Red meat supplies easily absorbed heme iron, supporting healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Meat and eggs are good sources of B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc from the meat helps immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: When sugar‑based sauces are limited, egg rolls fit well into low‑carb diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to egg whites.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Pork and beef contain saturated fats; moderation is advised for people with heart disease.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and seasonings can raise salt levels, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogens; ensure the filling is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the roll hot, sliced into bite‑size pieces. It can be enjoyed as a snack on its own or paired with rice, noodles and fresh vegetable salads. Add soy sauce, vinegar, chili sauce or a flavored mayo for extra taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked rolls in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Reheat in a steamer or skillet to retain crispness. Frozen rolls keep up to 1 month when wrapped tightly in plastic.

fish-sandwich-fried-on-white-bun-with-ch.title: Fish sandwich, fried, on white bun, with cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A fish sandwich is a fried piece of white fish placed between a split white bun and topped with melted cheese. Commonly used fish includes cod or pollock, and the bun is soft with a lightly toasted interior. The sandwich is served hot and often accompanied by sauces such as tartar or mayo.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first fish sandwich appeared in the United States in the early 1920s as a quick lunch for workers.
Traditionally the fish is coated in a batter of flour, eggs, and spices before frying.
The sandwich is often served with lemon wedges to brighten the fish flavor.
Some regions add fresh lettuce or pickles to the filling.
A plain white bun provides a neutral base, letting the fish and cheese shine.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Fried fish retains some omega‑3s, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: Source of high‑quality protein
items.content: Fish provides complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D in fish is important for bone health and immune function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Melted cheese adds calcium, helping to strengthen teeth and bones.

items.title: Energy‑dense meal
items.content: The combination of carbs, fats, and protein offers a quick energy boost.

items.title: Fish or dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, milk, or cheese.

items.title: High fat content from frying
items.content: Frying adds saturated fat and calories, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Risk of excess sodium
items.content: Salt used in the batter and sauces can be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Possible contaminants in fish
items.content: Certain fish may contain mercury or other toxins; choose reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is easy to eat by hand, though it can be cut in half for neatness. It is often served with fries, coleslaw, or fresh vegetables. Add your preferred sauce—tartar, mayo, or mustard—for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours, wrapped in foil or plastic wrap. Reheat in an oven or toaster to keep the bun crisp.

pasta-with-tomato-based-sauce-and-meat-h.title: Pasta with Tomato-Based Sauce and Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with tomato-based sauce and meat is a home recipe where cooked pasta is tossed with a fragrant sauce made from ripe tomatoes, onion, garlic, and sautéed meat (usually beef or pork). The dish is rich in carbohydrates, protein, and vitamins, featuring a robust flavor and inviting aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauce originated in Italy in the 19th century and quickly became a base for many pasta dishes.
Tomatoes used in the sauce are high in lycopene, an antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
Traditionally, the meat for the sauce is slow‑braised to become tender and infuse the sauce with flavor.
Different Italian regions add various herbs: basil, oregano, rosemary, or sage.
Al dente pasta retains a lower glycemic index than fully cooked pasta.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Pasta provides sustained energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Meat adds complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Lycopene and vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes supply lycopene and vitamin C, both antioxidants that support immune function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish contains iron, zinc, and potassium, important for blood formation and nerve function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Using whole‑grain pasta or adding vegetables boosts fiber content, aiding digestion.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The combination of pasta and meat can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Added salt in the sauce can increase sodium intake; use moderation.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional pasta contains wheat; people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose gluten‑free alternatives.

items.title: Meat fat content
items.content: Fatty cuts raise saturated fat levels; opting for lean cuts or trimming excess fat is recommended.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Cook pasta until al dente. Sauté finely chopped onion and garlic, add ground meat and brown it. Stir in tomato puree, diced tomatoes, and seasonings, then simmer 15‑20 minutes. Combine the sauce with the pasta, adding a splash of pasta cooking water if needed. Serve topped with grated Parmesan and fresh basil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked pasta in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze up to 2 months after cooling, using a freezer‑safe bag.

plantain-cooked-fat-added-ns-as-to-fat-t.title: Plantain, cooked, fat added, NS as to fat type

content.title: About
content.content: Plantain is a type of banana that is usually cooked before eating. When cooked with added fat (such as oil), it becomes tender, mildly sweet, and carries a fried aroma. This preparation is common in many world cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Plantain is often called the "cooking banana" because unlike sweet bananas it is rarely eaten raw.
In Africa, the Caribbean, and Southeast Asia plantains are fried, boiled, baked, or mashed.
Frying plantain in oil raises its calorie content but retains most B‑vitamins.
Plantain is rich in resistant starch, which benefits gut microbiota.
Traditional dishes in some cultures use plantain as a bread substitute.

items.title: High in potassium
items.content: Plantain provides a good amount of potassium, supporting normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C in plantain helps boost immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber and resistant starch promote healthy bowel movements.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates in plantain are quickly converted to energy, making it a good pre‑exercise food.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Plantain contains carotenoids and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Added fat increases the energy content, so portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Banana‑plantain allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to plantain.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salty oil or sauces are used, the sodium level can become elevated.

items.title: Glycemic index
items.content: Cooked plantain has a high glycemic index, which may affect blood sugar levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Plantain can be pan‑fried with a little oil, baked, steamed, or boiled. It is often served as a side dish, added to stews, salads, or mashed. For lighter flavor, season with garlic, paprika, or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw plantains in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Cooked plantain should be cooled to room temperature, then kept in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Soft salted pretzels are a yeast‑leavened baked snack shaped into knots, baked and then flash‑frozen. After thawing they retain a tender crumb and a characteristic salty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pretzels originated in Europe, traditionally made from rye flour.
Soft pretzels differ from crunchy ones by having a higher moisture content and often a steam‑baked crust.
Freezing preserves freshness and aroma without the need for preservatives.
The salt coating enhances flavor perception and helps form a slight crust when reheated.
In the United States soft pretzels are commonly served with cheese, mustard, or sweet dips.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat flour provides slowly released energy throughout the day.

items.title: Contains modest protein
items.content: Pretzels supply plant‑based protein that contributes to muscle maintenance.

items.title: Controlled sodium content
items.content: Sodium supports electrolyte balance, and the amount is regulated in the product.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many baked snacks, soft pretzels have a relatively low fat content.

items.title: Convenient energy source for athletes
items.content: Quick glycogen replenishment before or after training.

items.title: High sodium level
items.content: Excessive intake may contribute to elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Pretzels contain wheat, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although low in fat, the carbohydrate content makes them calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to wheat may experience reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thaw the pretzels in the microwave or at room temperature, then optionally warm them in an oven until lightly golden. Eat them as a snack, dip them in cheese sauce, mustard, hummus, or use them as a base for sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen pretzels in an airtight bag at –18 °C. Once thawed, consume within 2–3 days and store in the refrigerator.
